title: Successful v. Useful: Lessons on Teaching from Jim Collins and Peter Drucker
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. retells Jim Collins's visit to the modest home of the 86-year-old Peter Drucker, where Drucker told him that success is the wrong question and usefulness is the right one. Stuart draws four lessons for teachers. Success is self-centered while usefulness is other-oriented and often yields lasting success anyway. Professional anxieties are overwrought, since a teacher will probably survive losing a job. Living beneath one's means gives confidence and contentment. And leading business thinkers regard teaching as one of the most powerful human activities. The piece is a reflection on a teacher's purpose and professional posture rather than on technique.
points: Replaces the teacher's goal of success, as measured by tests, evaluations and awards, with the goal of being useful to others.
Argues that fear of losing a job or ranking last is exaggerated, borrowing Drucker's line that you will probably survive.
Links living beneath one's means to professional courage and lower anxiety.
Presents teaching as a calling that even elite management thinkers like Collins and Drucker saw themselves as practicing.
quotes: It seems to me you spend a lot of time worrying how you will survive,” said Peter. “You will probably survive.” He continued, “And you seem to spend a lot of energy on the question of how to be successful. But that is the wrong question.
What’s liberating about trying to be useful v. trying to be successful is that success is all about me, but usefulness is all about others.
This other-oriented life is almost entirely countercultural yet littered with the riches of a life well-lived.
We, too, fear that if we stop giving the evaluation rubric 100% of our professional attention, then surely we will lose our jobs or be relegated to last place in our schools.
I think we are also wise to live beneath our means, as this cultivates contentment in a discontented world and minimizes anxiety in an anxious one.
Drucker had figured out that you don’t need the trappings of success — titles, houses, fancy offices — to succeed at being useful.

Both Collins and Drucker view themselves as teachers. Rather than pursue the much more lucrative paths of CEO-ship that these men could have pursued, they instead dedicated their lives to be as useful as they could be to as many folks as possible.
